blocks.text: Here are the latest headlines from across Germany on Thursday, November 5:
November 5, 2026
Overall deportations down, but returns to Turkey on the rise

The number of people deported from Germany decreased by nearly 19% from January to September 2026 compared to the previous year, the Interior Ministry announced following a request from the Left Party.
Some 14,324 people were deported in the first nine months of this year, down from 17,651 in 2025. Turkey was the most common destination, followed by Georgia and Algeria.
The numbers reveal that deportations to Syria remain difficult due to the political situation there, even for convicted criminals. Six people have been returned there since the beginning of 2026.
Deportations to Turkey, however, appeared to buck the trend, as 2,025 people have been sent there.

According to the Interior Ministry, the number of foreign nationals leaving the country voluntarily has also slightly increased. Some 14,140 people have received assistance to return to their countries of origin, compared to 12,263 the year before.

articles.title: Navy probes alleged reservist over posts on San Andres youth riot
articles.summary: The Philippine Navy will look into online posts made by one of its alleged "reservists" on the recent street brawls at Manila’s San Andres district, warning that he could be dishonorably…

blocks.text: November 5, 2026 | 2:12pm
Philippine Navy

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Navy will look into online posts made by one of its alleged "reservists" on the recent street brawls at Manila’s San Andres district, warning that he could be dishonorably discharged if he is found to have violated military rules.

Navy spokesperson Capt. Marissa Martinez said in a statement that an “appropriate investigation” would be conducted to establish the accountability of a certain Aristotle Quitana, whom the Navy described as “reportedly” a member of its Reserve Force.
If the probe confirms a violation of military rules and regulations, Quitana “may face appropriate sanctions, including dishonorable discharge from the Reserve Force,” Martinez said.

“The Philippine Navy does not tolerate any remarks that incite violence or show disregard for human life, as these are contrary to the standards of discipline and core values expected of all Navy personnel, including members of the Reserve Force,” she added.
The Navy has not formally confirmed his reservist status.

Police have identified 14 minors involved in the disturbance that broke out early Tuesday along Diamante Street in Barangay 797, after the local police precinct received reports of a group of boys causing trouble.
Street fights have repeatedly broken out among youth groups in Manila where minors have been seen throwing bottles and wielding metal rods at each other.
Under the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act, children aged 15 and below are exempt from criminal liability, while those above 15 but below 18 can be held liable only if they acted with discernment.

Martinez said the Navy “remains committed to upholding the highest standards of discipline, accountability, and professionalism” among both regular and reserve personnel. The Navy did not give a timeline for the investigation.

articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has named Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda as the new Supreme Court (SC) chief justice.

blocks.text: Filtered By: Topstories
News
Published November 5, 2026 1:59pm
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has named Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda as the new Supreme Court (SC) chief justice.
He will be replacing Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo who will retire on November 6.
Zalameda was appointed as SC associate justice by then President Rodrigo Duterte on August 6, 2019.
Prior to this, he was an associate justice of the Court of Appeals for 11 years and served as the chairperson of its 17th Division.
He was also a branch clerk of the Makati Regional Trial Court.
Zalameda was appointed as City Prosecutor of Mandaluyong in 2002 and served as a public prosecutor in 1995.
He practiced law from 1990 to 1995.
Zalameda obtained his Bachelor of Laws Degree from the Ateneo de Manila University in 1987. He passed the Bar Examinations in 1988. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: US midterm elections 2026 live: Democrats eye historic upset in Mississippi Senate race as Republican blame game begins
articles.summary: Democrat Scott Colom is leading Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in the southern state; JD Vance pointed to the war in Iran as the ‘obvious’ culprit for Republicans’ loss

blocks.text: Mississippi count continues with Democratic candidate ahead by a razor-thin margin
Welcome to our continuing coverage of the 2026 midterms where almost 24 hours after Democrats secured their historic sweep of the US Congress, two Senate seats remain in play.

Counting in Alaska is expected to continue into Thursday, while in deep red Mississippi, Democrats could be close to pulling off another almighty upset. Currently, Democrat Scott Colom is leading his Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by just 1,138 votes with almost 96% of the vote counted.
In the last few hours, votes for Colom have been outpacing those for his Republican opponent, although new batches of votes have not been reported for several hours now.
Although a race this close would automatically trigger a recount in some states, Mississippi has no law on the books for initiating a recount.

blocks.caption: Mississippi Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom on Wednesday.  Photograph: Sue Dorfman/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Democrats haven’t won a US Senate seat in Mississippi since 1982, and Donald Trump carried the state by 22 points in 2024. It’s been much longer – not since 1875 – that the state elected a Black person to that office.

Colom is a seventh-generation Mississippian, whose father was a Republican who campaigned for Ronald Reagan and was friends with Thad Cochran, a longtime state politician. In 2015, he unseated a nearly 30-year incumbent when he was elected the first Black district attorney for the 16th circuit. As district attorney, he had a 94% success rate for convictions.
Meanwhile, after Democrats secured their historic wins in last night’s midterm elections, Republicans are beginning the blame game:

items: Donald Trump claimed Republicans fared poorly because he was not on the ballot – after repeatedly urging voters to pretend he was on the ballot.
JD Vance pointed to Trump’s ongoing war in Iran as the “obvious” culprit for the loss.

Pete Hegseth’s role leading the unpopular war could lead to him taking the fall – despite Trump publicly backing him. Republicans including Trump foe Thomas Massie have criticized the defense secretary.

Ron DeSantis, Florida’s governor, said the “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans” was caused in part by his party failing to target their ad spending on issues that would motivate voters.

blocks.text: According to exit polls from the Associated Press, voters said the cost of living and government corruption were their two top issues. But how will Trump cope with this new political reality?
The Guardian’s David Smith explores that – and whether these elections mark the beginning of the end for Trump – this analysis piece here:

articles.title: Marcos appoints Zalameda as chief justice
articles.summary: Zalameda, 63, will replace Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo, who will reach compulsory retirement on November 6.

blocks.text: November 5, 2026 | 1:53pm
MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has appointed Supreme Court Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda as the 28th chief justice of the Supreme Court.
Zalameda, 63, will replace Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo, who will reach compulsory retirement on November 6.
The appointment was announced by Presidential Communications Office chief Lino Cayetano in a press briefing on Thursday, November 5.
Zalameda will be the first chief justice appointed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., after former President Rodrigo Duterte appointed Gesmundo in 2021.
Marcos chose him after two appointees of former President Benigno Aquino III and two other justices appointed by Duterte.
Duterte appointed him to the Supreme Court on Aug. 6, 2019.
Prior to his Supreme Court stint, he previously served as an associate justice of the Court of Appeals, where he later chaired its 17th Division.

articles.title: PH to flag all shipments from Laos after P1.36-B shabu seizure -- DILG
articles.summary: The Philippines will flag all shipments originating from Laos following the seizure of some P1.36 billion worth of shabu at a Manila port, Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said…

blocks.text: Published November 5, 2026 1:05pm

The Philippines will flag all shipments originating from Laos following the seizure of some P1.36 billion worth of shabu at a Manila port, the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) said Thursday.
"Ngayon ifa-flag na namin lahat ng shipment galing Laos, ifa-flag namin kung may drugs talaga kasi ginagawa nila tinatago nila kapag papunta rito," DILG Secretary Jonvic Remulla said in an interview.
(Now we will flag all shipments from Laos, we will flag if there are drugs because they are doing it and hiding it when they deliver here.)
According to Remulla, the discovery of shabu concealed inside cardboard packaging was something he had not encountered before.
Drug syndicates may be looking for alternative routes to bring illegal drugs into the country, Remulla said, after authorities intercepted around 17 tons of illegal drugs in open waters.

Meanwhile, Remulla questioned why authorities had seized nearly one ton of illegal drugs through Philippine ports over the past four years but no similar seizures were recorded in the six years before 2022, except for the so-called magnetic lifter shipment.
"To prove to you na nakakalusot, the price of drugs in 2019 to 2020 was P3,800 per gram. Ngayon P6,800 per gram so umakyat ang presyo. Ibig sabihin supply is depleted, 'di ba bumaba," he said.

(To prove to you that it is slipping through, the price of drugs in 2019 to 2020 was P3,800 per gram. Now it is P6,800 per gram so the price has gone up. It means supply is depleted, hasn't it gone down.)
"Bakit nakakalusot at sino nagpapasulot dati sa ports ng Manila," he added.
(Why is it slipping through and who is allowing it at ports of Manila.)
On Wednesday, authorities seized some 200 kilograms of shabu worth P1.36 billion from a shipment originating from Laos at the Manila International Container Port (MICP) in North Harbor, Manila.

The shipment reportedly traveled from Laos to Haiphong in Vietnam, before heading to Hong Kong. The container van was transferred to another vessel in Hong Kong before being shipped to the Philippines.
Authorities are also probing the alleged links of several Filipinos to the attempt to smuggle 521 kilograms of shabu from Laos to the Philippines via private jet last October. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Bring it on’: Pauline Hanson to appeal Mehreen Faruqi racial discrimination ruling in high court
articles.summary:
One Nation leader granted special leave to appeal after full federal court earlier this year agreed Hanson portrayed Faruqi as a ‘second-class citizen’

  • Get our

blocks.text: Australia’s high court has agreed to hear Pauline Hanson’s appeal against a ruling that she engaged in racial discrimination against Mehreen Faruqi when she told the Greens senator to “pack your bags and piss off back to Pakistan”.
The One Nation leader was granted special leave to appeal on Thursday after the full federal court earlier this year unanimously upheld a 2024 decision.
The high court will examine whether Hanson’s comments breached the Racial Discrimination Act (RDA) or if the federal court decision impeded her implied freedom of speech.
Hanson welcomed the decision on social media, saying “this case has always been bigger than me and bigger than one tweet”.
“Australians must be able to speak their minds, question their government and disagree with each other without being frightened into silence,” the 72-year-old senator wrote.
“That freedom is under attack, including through Labor’s digital duty of care bill and its threat to lawful debate online.”
Faruqi said in a statement on Thursday: “Bring it on.”
“This has been a long, hard road walked alongside everyone who has been targeted by racism. We won’t be backing down now,” the Greens senator wrote.

“The highest court in Australia can now determine once and for all that people in this country are protected against racism. People of colour, migrants and Muslims deserve to feel safe in the place they call home. In times like these where we are being attacked and demonised, our legal system must be able to provide protection against vilification.”
A spokesperson for the federal attorney general, Michelle Rowland, said section 18C of the RDA was more important to Australia’s social cohesion “than ever”.

“As the matter is before the court, it would be inappropriate to comment further,” the spokesperson said. “The Australian government’s position is clear: there is no place for racism or racial hatred in our society.”
The dispute arose in 2022 after the death of Queen Elizabeth II.
after newsletter promotion

Faruqi tweeted: “Condolences to those who knew the Queen. I cannot mourn the leader of a racist empire built on stolen lives, land and wealth of colonised peoples. We are reminded of the urgency of Treaty with First Nations, justice & reparations for British colonies & becoming a republic.”

In response, Hanson posted: “Your attitude appalls and disgusts me. When you immigrated to Australia you took every advantage of this country. You took citizenship, bought multiple homes, and a job in a parliament. It’s clear you’re not happy, so pack your bags and piss off back to Pakistan – PH.”

Justice Angus Stewart in November 2024 found Hanson’s tweet was unlawful and portrayed Faruqi as a “second-class citizen” who took advantage of Australia and who, as a migrant to the country, “should be grateful for what she has and keep quiet” – a position he declared to be “exclusionary”.

Stewart found Hanson’s comment that Faruqi should “piss off back to Pakistan” was a “variant of the slogan ‘go back to from where you came from’”, which he said was a “racist trope” and a “strong form of racism”. He added that Hanson’s tweet, given her profile, likely “empowered others” to make similar or worse comments.

The judge rejected Hanson’s arguments, including that Faruqi’s tweet on the queen’s death justified her response. He found Hanson’s tweet did not fall within the fair comment exemption because it was an “angry, personal attack”.
Stewart’s judgment was unanimously upheld in July this year by the three federal court judges Melissa Perry, Geoffrey Kennett and Elizabeth Bennett.

articles.title: UK found to be ‘dangerously’ reliant on China for critical minerals needed for defence and AI
articles.summary:
Delivering net zero also at risk, say MPs as they call for centralised policy and funding for mines and diversification

The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials…

blocks.text: The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.

MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.

“Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy,” said the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne. “We cannot rearm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.
“Yet 16 years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed.”
It is the second time in a week that the government’s policy on China has been criticised by Byrne’s committee.

China has a stranglehold on the world’s supply of rare earths and other critical minerals, as well as their refined byproducts that are used in everything from military jets to car-locking systems and consumer products such as fridges and washing machines.

The committee heard that “the processing stage” was where the bottlenecks were, with China dominating the refining of seven categories of minerals, including refined lithium needed for electric vehicles and rare earths used in the fuselage and wings of military aircraft to help withstand temperature extremes.
MPs were told that demand for lithium alone would increase 45-fold between now and 2030, leaving the UK in a high-risk dependency relationship with China.
The demand for rare earths needed for permanent magnets used in military jets and other applications would rise 16-fold in the same period as Britain was seeking to rebuild its military capabilities.

But with China capable of suddenly turning off rare earth supplies, as it did in 2025, a dependency on Beijing was a strategic vulnerability for the UK economy and national security, the committee found.
Separate restrictions on legacy chips after a row over a Dutch intervention in the China-owned Nexperia left the European car industry “days away” from stoppages last October.

The EU, the US and other countries faced the same risk of supplies of rare earths being cut off by China, and the committee said the UK was not putting enough effort into finding alternative supplies.

Donald Trump secured a one-year reprieve on global export restrictions on rare earths from Xi Jinping in October last year. This was extended to January 2027 after the Chinese president’s recent visit to Washington.
However, the reprieve means the UK is at the mercy of US-China relations, the report suggests.
after newsletter promotion
The most “realistic” solution was for the UK to work closely with G7 partners, the rest of Europe and Indo-Pacific countries, to “aggregate demand” and bring in new suppliers.
The committee said its investigation was frustrated by lack of transparency by the government.
“Parliament has no visibility of the capabilities the government is seeking to protect, the vulnerabilities it has identified, or the projects it is backing to reduce risk,” it said.

The committee has drawn up a 10-point plan that includes: working to identify domestic mining; refining and recycling opportunities and their costs; a strategy to encourage business to reduce procurement from China; a plan to unlock investment; and assess planning and permitting processes that may prove a barrier to mining.
As it stood, the committee said it could not be confident the government could satisfy any of its 10 tests.
“The UK requires new institutional and financial muscle,” it concluded.
A government spokesperson denied it did not have a critical minerals strategy saying it was delivering £400m “to ramp up domestic production and recycling” and forge new international partnerships.

“Our strategy also sets clear goals for 2035, including meeting 10% of demand through domestic production and 20% through recycling, with no more than 60% of any critical minerals coming from any single country,” they added.

articles.title: Protesters to join nationwide march as France braces for day of strike action
articles.summary:
Hospital workers, air traffic and rail staff expected to join strikes amid renewed protests over education and rising living costs

Hundreds of thousands are expected to march in…

blocks.text: Hundreds of thousands are expected to march in demonstrations across France as trade unions call for a nationwide strike expected to extend to hospital workers, air traffic control, the post office, teachers and rail staff.

President Emmanuel Macron’s final months in office continue to be marred by domestic crises, as high school students protesting over poor teaching conditions have been joined by workers in weekly protests over the cost of living. Meanwhile, the government is struggling to pass a belt-tightening budget in a divided parliament as public debt approaches 120% of economic output.

Ahead of Thursday’s strike action, France’s four main rail unions said that the government’s proposed budget cuts would “worsen poverty, slash social security, freeze state workers’ salaries and dry up investment needed for environmental measures”.

Amid the renewed protests centred on living costs, public spending cuts and the troubled education system, the far-right, anti-immigration candidate Marine Le Pen is polling high for the 2027 presidential election to replace Macron next spring.

High school students continued to blockade schools over overcrowded classes and dilapidated buildings, saying the government’s proposed measures on capping some class sizes and loaning funds to regional authorities to fix schools were not enough. University students joined in blockading some faculties. Trade unions from across the political landscape joined in a call for strikes over the rising cost of living, with private schools’ teachers unions also joining strikes alongside state school teachers.

blocks.caption: French soldiers patrol a street in Paris on the eve of the strikes. Rights’ groups objected to the ‘authoritarian’ attempt by Macron’s executive to clamp down on the right to demonstrate. Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

blocks.text: Rights’ groups protested over what they said was heavy policing and an “authoritarian” attempt by Macron’s executive to clamp down on the right to demonstrate.

The French Human Rights League said there was an “authoritarian shift” to stifle “any dissenting voice” as the government put in place heavy policing and authorities issued restrictions on demonstrating in city centres, as well as curfews in certain areas.

Sophie Binet, the head of the leftwing CGT union, said: “We’re living at a very serious time with a very dangerous authoritarian drift from the government”, criticising decisions by authorities in cities such as Rennes, Toulouse and Lyon to push demonstrations out of city centres.
after newsletter promotion
Marylise Léon, the head of the moderate CFDT trade union, said: “The principle of a demonstration is its visibility.”

The national rail operator SNCF said there would be “disturbances” to train services on regional lines and some parts of the greater Paris area. Dockers said there would be disruption in French ports. The education ministry said it expected almost 18% of nursery and primary school teachers to strike. Trade unions said they also expected secondary teachers to take part in Thursday’s strike.

articles.title: ‘An insult to his culture’: Italian chef sacked for not putting pineapple on pizza loses bid to get job back
articles.summary:
Australia’s Fair Work Commission heard that Davide Tamburella was sacked for refusing to use the controversial topping

With its sea foam-green and white decor, exposed brick columns and…

blocks.text: With its sea foam-green and white decor, exposed brick columns and “classic Italian dishes” served atop European oak tables, La Costa was billed as an elegant slice of Italy in the urban heart of Queensland, Australia’s sunshine state.
“We promise, it’ll only take a moment to realize you’re not in Brisbane anymore, you’ve made it to the Italian Riviera,” the now closed restaurant’s website still reads.

But for its ​​disgruntled former head chef, it seems, just one moment – or, more specifically, one ingredient – was all it took to break the spell conjuring the “luxurious splendor of Italy’s coastline” and to plonk his diners right back into the nightclub district of Queensland’s Fortitude Valley.
That ingredient was pineapple. On a pizza.

A Fair Work Commission ruling filed on Tuesday heard that Davide Tamburella was sacked from La Costa on 20 May this year, a fortnight after he was hauled before his boss, Elliot Ingram, “to address performance concerns”.
Among those concerns was the Italian chef’s refusal to put pineapple on pizza – on the grounds that to do so was “an insult to his culture”.
In the Australian state, in which the spiky tropical fruit is so revered that a giant (or at least big) monument has been built in its honour, it is this refusal that many would consider a sacrilege.
But for both Tamburella and Ingram, this would prove a costly refusal.

blocks.caption: Alfresco dining in Italy. Ham and pineapple pizza not pictured. Photograph: AsiaDreamPhoto/Alamy

blocks.text: The Italian was more than three years into a 186 visa process – an employer-sponsored pathway to permanent residency. Ingram says he waited as long as he legally could to notify authorities that he was no longer hiring Tamburella in the hope that the Italian’s visa application would be approved before the restaurateur was legally obliged to withdraw his sponsorship. It did not, meaning the temporary migrant would have to start the 186 process again.
For Ingram, there was the cost of doing business.
“We had a large function come in, and they were spending in excess of $15,000, and the guy paying for the whole thing says: ‘Look, I need to get some ham and pineapple pizza’,” Ingram said.

The Fair Work Commission heard that Tamburella acknowledged that this was the third time he had refused this direction, instead requesting Ingram “check how important it is for Italians not to put pineapple on a pizza”.

And while Ingram says the divisive tropical pizza was not his own first choice, he says that 17 years in hospitality and more than a decade of running restaurants has taught him to “pick your battles”.

“Do I go and buy a ham and pineapple pizza? It’s probably not my absolute favourite,” he said, tactfully. “But I’m not going to turn my nose up at it, that’s for sure. And, look, we have had ham and pineapple pizza on the kid’s menu previously.”

Tamburella alleged that he was terminated in contravention of the Fair Work Act, with his dismissal partly motivated by him suffering a workplace injury after he struck a metal handrail, fracturing his right hand in two places.
The FWC commissioner, Jennifer Hunt, dismissed Tamburella’s general protections application on the grounds that it was filed too late and did not meet the criteria for exceptional circumstances.
La Costa closed in July when its lease expired, with Ingram citing the high cost of doing business in Fortitude Valley.
Tamburella was contacted for comment. He is now employed at another Italian restaurant. Pineapple does not appear on their menu.

articles.title: NASA's Swift space telescope plunges back to Earth in fiery demise
articles.summary: NASA's Swift orbital observatory fell back to Earth after running its mission for more than two decades. A rescue attempt to raise its sinking orbit had earlier failed.

image.caption: Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory — equipped with three telescopes — was launched into orbit in 2004Image: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab

blocks.text: A premier NASA space telescope met a fiery end as it crashed back to Earth — two decades after its launch — following the failure of a rescue mission.
The unmanned Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory re-entered the Earth's atmosphere over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia on Wednesday at 7.39 am EST (12.39 pm UTC), the US space agency said.
Most of the spacecraft was expected to have burnt up as it traveled through the atmosphere, NASAsaid, adding that some components may have survived re-entry.
What was NASA's Swift mission?
NASA's prized Swift observatory — equipped with three telescopes — was launched into orbit in 2004.

The observatory was tasked with studying gamma ray bursts, the biggest ​energy blasts in universe for two years. But its mission spanned 11 times longer than planned, lasting just a few days short of 22 years.
The $500 million (€444 million) Swift satellite weighed roughly 1,452 kilograms (3,200 pounds).
It studied hundreds of supernova explosions, star-shredding black holes, stellar X-ray flares, asteroids and ​comets.
Swift also contributed to nearly 7,000 published scientific ⁠papers.
Failed attempt to rescue Swift observatory
The satellite, which was in a good condition, fell out of orbit partly due to powerful geomagnetic storms set off by solar eruptions.
In July, NASA roped in private company Katalyst Space and launched a mission to raise the altitude of the Swift observatory.
But Katalyst Space's three-armed robotic servicing spacecraft — called LINK — faced issues with attitude control soon after reaching space, causing it to spin uncontrollably.
The rescue vehicle plunged back to Earth in September, while Swift ceased operations on October 20.
There were no immediate reports of damage on ground as the Swift observatory fell back to its home planet.

articles.title: South Korea says it will expand naval operations closer to strait of Hormuz
articles.summary:
Seoul to seek parliamentary approval to extend anti-piracy Cheonghae unit’s area to about 650km from the vital strait after criticism from Donald Trump on Iran war support

South Korea plans…

blocks.text: South Korea plans to expand the operations ⁠of its anti-piracy unit to waters closer to the strait of Hormuz, its defence ministry has said, after pressure from Donald Trump to ⁠provide support for his war in Iran.

The government is to submit a motion to parliament that would expand the Cheonghae unit’s area of operation to waters near the port of Duqm in Oman, which ​is about 650km (403 miles) away from the strait. The motion also needs to be approved by ‌President Lee Jae Myung and the cabinet.
“The enhancement of the Cheonghae unit’s mission is to protect our citizens and safeguard our economic interests,” a defence ministry official told reporters.
The reinforcement was strictly for non-combat purposes and the unit would operate independently of allied forces, said the official, speaking on condition of anonymity.

“Operations will remain restricted to the open waters south of Oman, and the maritime patrol aircraft will be prohibited from targeting or monitoring Iranian territory, territorial waters or the interior of the strait of Hormuz during their missions,” he said.

Trump has criticised Seoul for what he called insufficient support for the Iran war and scaled back major joint ⁠military drills by the two countries’ armed forces this summer, a move that ​unsettled the US ally.
The unit has been stationed in the Gulf of Aden since 2009 to ensure safe navigation of commercial vessels.
The motion also seeks to ​extend the unit’s deployment to the Middle ‌East, which is set ‌to expire at the end of 2026, a ministry spokesperson said, confirming a report by Yonhap ‌news agency.
It currently includes a 4,400-ton-class destroyer, a maritime operations helicopter, up to three rigid-hull inflatable boats and about 300 service members, according to broadcaster YTN.
Seoul would also deploy a P-8A maritime patrol aircraft and increase the unit’s personnel by 75, the Korea Herald reported.
South ​Korea relies heavily on oil ​imports and sourced 70% of its supplies from the Middle East in ​2025, most of ‌it delivered through the ​strait of Hormuz, ​according to the industry ministry.

Lee said on 18 September that he would not deploy military assets to the Middle East in a way that could draw the country into conflict, but that Seoul was reviewing playing a greater role in safeguarding navigation in the region.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Joshua Wong, face of Hong Kong's pro-democracy protests, jailed for 10 years
articles.summary: Wong, 30, is among hundreds of Hongkongers detained under the controversial national security law.

blocks.text: Wong, who turned 30 last month, has already been imprisoned multiple times for his activism which started when he was a teen.
On Thursday, he arrived in court wearing a dark blue long-sleeved shirt, khaki trousers and black-rimmed glasses. He looked slimmer compared to his previous public appearances.
He nodded in greeting towards members of the packed public gallery, and took notes intermittently as the judge read out the reasons for his sentencing.
A crowd had gathered outside the court, with dozens of Hongkongers having queued for hours hoping to get a seat in the public gallery. There was also a heavy police presence.
Wong is already serving time for subversion and was due to be freed early next year when he was handed the latest charges, which he has pleaded guilty to earlier in September.
Two months and two days of the 10-year term will be served concurrently with his ongoing sentence, the judge said on Thursday.
Prosecutors said that Wong had conspired with other campaigners, including self-exiled activist Nathan Law, to lobby for foreign sanctions and blockades against Beijing.
These activities took place between July and late November 2020, the court heard.
Wong and Law had been co-founders of Demosisto, a now defunct pro-democracy political party.
Wong's friend and fellow activist Frances Hui, now based in the US, says she is "heartbroken" and "outraged" by the verdict.

"Today's sentencing is not just about Joshua. It is part of a broader political crackdown that seeks to rewrite a chapter of Hong Kong's history and erase the contributions of an entire generation who believed they could shape the future of their city," she told the BBC.
Human Rights Watch described the ruling as "cruel and unjust".

"To keep Hong Kong society subdued, and to reduce the chance of an international outcry, the Hong Kong government appears to have adopted the tactic of stacking charges against influential pro-democracy leaders," said its Asia director Elaine Pearson.

The harshest sentence under the controversial national security law (NSL) thus far has been handed to former media tycoon Jimmy Lai, who was jailed for 20 years, also for colluding with foreign forces.
Born to IT professional Roger and homemaker Grace in October 1996, Wong was diagnosed with dyslexia as a child, which made him struggle with school.

However, he was quick to challenge established rules and norms when they didn't make sense. In secondary school, he rallied with his classmates to protest against the high prices of canteen lunches on Facebook.
In 2011, Wong, then 14, co-founded the pro-democracy student activist group Scholarism, which quickly grew in size and influence.
The following year, the group rallied more than 100,000 people to protest against Hong Kong's plans to implement mandatory "patriotic education" in schools, forcing the authorities to back down.

By 2014, Wong, who was then at the forefront of a civil disobedience movement known as the "Umbrella Movement", had already become one of the most recognisable faces of Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement.
In 2016, he co-founded Demosisto with Law and Agnes Chow, an activist who is now also in exile.
But he often expressed discomfort at being labelled a "protest leader".
"We have a lot of facilitators in this movement and I'm one of them... Instead of having a top-down command, we now have a bottom-up command hub," Wong told The Financial Times in November 2019.
Demosisto disbanded in 2020, the year Beijing introduced the NSL in Hong Kong.

Law left for the UK and continued his advocacy abroad, while Wong stayed on in Hong Kong and tried to run for a seat in its legislature – but was barred, with authorities citing his opposition to the NSL as one of the reasons.
Meanwhile, the court cases against Wong were stacking up.
On 23 November 2020, he pleaded guilty to several charges related to his involvement in protests outside the Hong Kong police headquarters in 2019.

Then came the NSL charges. While still in prison in February 2021, Wong was among 47 people charged with "conspiracy to commit subversion". The group became known as the Hong Kong 47 and remains the largest prosecution so far under the NSL.
Wong was still serving his 56-month sentence for the subversion conviction when he was charged with collusion under the NSL last year.

On 22 November 2020, the day before he pleaded guilty to the protest charges, Wong wrote in a post on Instagram addressed to "the people of Hong Kong": "To be honest, I have never had much faith in Hong Kong's politics, but I have every confidence in the people of Hong Kong.
"Even as political power now poses a comprehensive challenge to the resilience of our civil society, I believe the people of Hong Kong will, as always, find a way to see things through."
Additional reporting by Martin Yip

articles.title: Prominent Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in 2nd national security case
articles.summary: Prominent Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years in prison Thursday for his second conviction under a Beijing-imposed national security law, in a case that critics say reflects the…

image.caption: Pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong, seen here in October 2019, was sentenced for a second conviction in Hong Kong on Thursday. (Vincent Yu/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Prominent Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years in prison Thursday for his second conviction under a Beijing-imposed national security law, in a case that critics say reflects the crackdown on the city's once-thriving pro-democracy movement.
Wong is already serving a near 5-year prison term for his part in the city's biggest national security case

Wong was charged in 2025 with conspiracy to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security under the law. In September he pleaded guilty to the offence, a move that can typically reduce the sentence.

The 30-year-old is already serving a four-year, eight-month prison term for the city's biggest national security case after entering a guilty plea. Before being prosecuted for the collusion-related charge, Wong had been expected to be freed in January 2027.

Judge William Tam said during the sentencing hearing that Wong's offence was of a grave nature and rejected that his role was limited. He also said he considered a 13-year prison sentence as a starting point but reduced it because of Wong's guilty plea.
Wong looked calm and thanked his supporters before leaving the court. His supporters waved to him and Tiffany Chin, a former member of the now-disbanded Scholarism, once led by Wong, was in tears.
The judge said Wong could serve his two prison sentences concurrently. Wong only has about two months left on the sentence for his previous national security conviction.
Supporters attend court

Some members of the public started queuing outside the court building as early as Tuesday to secure a seat in the public gallery. Activist Lui Yuk-lin held a piece of paper carrying Wong's name in the line Thursday.

Resident ET Wong said that when Joshua Wong was just teenager, he possessed "big-picture thinking" that some adults might not even have. He walked a difficult path for Hong Kong's future, human rights and student movement, she said.
"At least in my heart, he should not have spent a single day in wrongful imprisonment," she said.
People line up outside Hong Kong's High Court ahead of a Thursday morning sentencing. (Tyrone Siu/Reuters)
Chilling dissent

Hong Kong once had a freewheeling civil society marked by its vibrant protest and media scenes. But after an anti-government movement rocked the city in 2019, authorities reduced public choice in elections and arrested many leading activists. Some news outlets known for their reports critical of the government shut down and dozens of civil society groups dissolved.
Observers say Wong's sentencing shows the authorities' determination to keep prominent activists in prison for as long as possible, further chilling civic activism.

"NSL charges can be repeatedly weaponized to keep a specific political prisoner in jail, if the government deems necessary," said Eric Lai, a research fellow at Georgetown Center for Asian Law, referring to the national security law.

items: Hong Kong's new security law expands scope abroad. What to know about the Article 23 laws
Hong Kong activist Agnes Chow still fears Beijing's reach despite living in Canada

blocks.text: But Beijing views Wong as an anti-China figure supporting Hong Kong independence, a stance that crosses its red line. Hong Kong authorities also said the security law is crucial for the city's stability following the 2019 protests, maintaining that the city's law enforcement actions were evidence-based.

Wong, second from left, with activists Eddie Chu, Owen Chow and Lester Shum, posing with signs in support of the 12 Hong Kong activists held in mainland China after attempting to flee the city for Taiwan, in Hong Kong, October 20, 2020. (Lam Yik/Reuters)
Prosecution focused on Wong's lobbying and advocacy

The prosecution previously alleged that Wong and fellow activist Nathan Law had agreed in or around 2016 to lobby internationally to achieve their goal of democratic self-determination. It said that before the security law was introduced, the pair had been calling for sanctions and other adverse measures against Hong Kong and China. It pointed to his meetings with U.S. politicians like Nancy Pelosi and Marco Rubio in 2016 and 2019.

After the law was enacted, Law and others advanced their work abroad by meeting foreign politicians and launching petition drives, it said. Wong supported the effort from Hong Kong through foreign media outlets and social media to draw foreign countries' attention and bolster the request for sanctions, blockade or other hostile measures against China and Hong Kong, it said.
His lawyer Derek Chan earlier urged the court to impose a sentence that would give his client some hope, adding that Wong wishes to take care of his parents after his release.
China hasn't 'imprisoned his spirit': Jimmy Lai's son on father's sentencing
His friends said during his nearly six years in prison, Wong has kept reading books and exercising, teaching himself guitar while maturing in his thinking.
To his supporters, Wong is a political star representing a younger generation born in the final years of Hong Kong's British colonial rule before the city's return to China in 1997.
Despite being held behind bars, Wong's influence appears to have remained a concern, at least for the pro-Beijing camp.

In September, a pro-Beijing newspaper report criticized a 2017 documentary about Wong on Netflix for "beautifying" his crimes. The city's security bureau told local media the government was taking follow-up action.
But the documentary then shot to the top of Netflix's popular chart in Hong Kong.

articles.title: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
articles.summary: The vice-president's blunt assessment of Republican election defeat marked one of the sharpest breaks with a sitting president in recent memory.

blocks.text: With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?
By
Washington correspondent

Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.
In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election.
"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."
In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.

Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington. While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.
But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.
Could Democrats in Congress end the war in Iran?
Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.

It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.

Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices.

blocks.caption: JD Vance walks on a stage. An American flag is behind him

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Drawing contrasts with Trump will be a delicate balancing act if Vance seeks the presidency, Byman added.
That balance was on display in Vance's post. The vice president didn't mention Trump by name and attributed much of his election results analysis to unnamed pollsters.
Vance "put his toe in the water to see what he's going to do," Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.

Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan: "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."
The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech.
The BBC has contacted Vance's office for comment.
Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over.
It's also up for debate exactly how much Vance broke from Trump. Vance showed the message to Trump before posting it online, according to The New York Times.
Trump, for his part, could change his mind and make clear he'll brook no dissent from Vance or anyone else.

The president has been circumspect about who he'd support to succeed him as the 2028 Republican presidential nominee. Trump has praised Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on several occasions, but hasn't said when - or if – he'd make an endorsement.

The president appears to relish the guessing game of who he'd back to carry on his political movement, even in the past floating the idea that he'd continue to a third term (which is barred by the US Constitution).
Vance's midterms missive might not be that significant in the end. Or it could have been the starting gun for the 2028 race and the battle for the post-Trump Republican Party.
Nardine Saad contributed reporting.

articles.title: Valkyries celebrate WNBA championship with San Francisco and Oakland fans
articles.summary: Dancing in the streets, popping champagne and high-fiving fans was all part of the celebration on Wednesday as the Golden State Valkyries parade made its way through Oakland and then across the bay…

image.caption: Golden State Valkyries' Kaitlyn Chen sprays champagne toward fans during the team's WNBA championship parade in San Francisco Wednesday. (Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Photos

Dancing in the streets, popping champagne and high-fiving fans was all part of the celebration on Wednesday as the Golden State Valkyries parade made its way through Oakland and then across the bay in San Francisco.
The team honoured fans on both sides of the bay as they celebrated their victory Wednesday
The newest WNBA champs encouraged their California fans to call in sick, skip out on work or ditch school Wednesday — and elated basketball fans appeared thrilled to take their advice.
Tens of thousands of people lined the streets for a Golden State Valkyries victory parade after the team sealed the championship on Saturday in a 68-63 Game 7 win over the Atlanta Dream.

There was dancing, champagne, team colours and plenty of high-fives. And of course, team mascot Vi. She's a raven, commonly seen as a sidekick to Valkyries in Norse mythology, according to the team website.
Golden State Valkyries mascot Violet, also known as Vi, rides on a float during the team's WNBA championship parade. (Darren Yamashita/Imagn Images/Reuters)
Oakland to San Francisco

The Valkyries began their day of celebration at Oakland's Jack London Square, not far from the team's downtown practice facility, then took a ferry across the bay to begin the parade from San Francisco's Ferry Building.
It concluded near the San Francisco Giants' Oracle Park.
Golden State Valkyries centre Kiah Stokes at the parade kickoff rally at Jack London Square in Oakland, Calif. (Yalonda M. James/San Francisco Chronicle/The Asscociated Press)
The players posed for photos onstage with the WNBA championship trophy at Jack London Square in Oakland before hopping on a ferry across San Francisco Bay. (Darren Yamashita/Imagn Images/Reuters)
Valkyries forward Kayla Thornton. (Darren Yamashita/Imagn Images/Reuters)
Year 2 championship
Golden State was granted an expansion franchise three years ago. At the time, team owner Joe Lacob guaranteed a championship within five years.

His promise was honoured as the team led by coach Natalie Nakase delivered an improbable title in Year 2 after becoming the first expansion franchise to reach the playoffs in its inaugural year in 2025.
Fans turned out for the parade in the team's colours from head to toe. (Darren Yamashita/Imagn Images/Reuters)
Valkyries fans cheered from a rooftop as the parade rolled past. (Darren Yamashita/Imagn Images/Reuters)
'Too small' goes big
After the Dream beat the Valkyries in Game 3, Atlanta player Angel Reese taunted the Valkyries' bench with a hand gesture for "too small."
But some Valkyries turned the taunt into a power move after their victory, and brought it out for the parade.
Valkyries guard Juste Jocyte gives the 'too small' gesture, started by Angel Reese in Game 3, to the fans during the Valkyries parade. (David Gonzales/Imagn Images/Reuters)
Valkyries guard Tiffany Hayes celebrated from the double decker bus as it made its way through San Francisco. (Darren Yamashita/Imagn Images/Reuters)

articles.title: Fuel, transport costs push inflation to 7.8% in October 2026
articles.summary: The PSA reported that headline inflation accelerated to 7.8% in October, marking the highest figure since February 2023, when it reached 8.6%.

blocks.text: November 5, 2026 | 11:31am

A gas station in Quezon City on Aug. 16, 2026 offers additional fuel discounts to partner public utility vehicle (PUV) drivers, on top of the recent increase of government fuel subsidy, to help lessen the burden of high fuel cost.
The Philippine STAR / Miguel de Guzman
MANILA, Philippines — Headline inflation accelerated to 7.8% in October, marking the highest figure since February 2023, when it reached 8.6%.

The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) reported on Thursday, November 5, that transport costs primarily drove the uptrend, with the index surging to 20.1% from 14.6% in September. Higher fuel prices also pushed up housing, water, electricity and gas indices to 9.3% from 8.4% in the previous month.
Food inflation, meanwhile, eased slightly to 6.4% from 6.8%, owing to slower annual increases in the indices of fish and vegetables.
Faster increases, however, were still seen in rice and corn prices, with inflation accelerating to 20.7% from 20.3% and 19.3% from 17.3%, respectively.
Core inflation also rose to 5.4%. An increase in the metric, which excludes volatile food and energy items, suggests broader price pressures affecting the country's economy.
The peso's purchasing power has been on a downward trend since January. Data from the statistics agency showed that a peso in September 2026 was worth only P0.68 relative to its 2018 base value.
As long as inflation remains above the central bank's 3% target, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) says the country will remain on a tightening cycle.
The central bank raised its key policy rate by 50 basis points to 5.5% in October, bringing total rate hikes to 125 basis points this year alone.
The BSP will next meet on December 17 and release its final monetary policy report on December 23.

articles.title: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case
articles.summary:
Wong, 30, has been imprisoned since 2020 and is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under national security law

Hong Kong activist

blocks.text: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong was sentenced on Thursday to 10 years in prison after pleading guilty to “foreign collusion”, his second conviction under a national security law that critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.

Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s 2014 pro-democracy demonstrations, submitted his plea in September. He had been accused of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.
In his ruling, High ​court Judge William Tam ‌described Wong’s actions as “grave in nature”.

He said Wong had visited the US to seek foreign interference ahead of the national security law’s introduction in 2020, and continued to share posts on social media by Law calling for sanctions after it was enacted.
Wong’s role was to “supply his underground support” and “arouse the attention of foreign countries to bolster the cause” of exiled activists, the judge said.
He said Wong’s sentence will run concurrently with the remaining term of his previous national security offence.
Wong wore a dark blue shirt and thick rimmed glasses in court, and nodded and bowed as supporters waved.

The former student leader is already serving a prison term of four years and eight months, imposed in November 2024, for conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.

Wong, 30, gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests, which paralysed the city’s financial centre and galvanised a generation of young people. In October 2014, he appeared – with his trademark black-rimmed spectacles – on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.

When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the protests and immediately took to the streets.

The following year, Beijing introduced a sweeping national security law it said was needed to restore stability to the former British colony, but critics say has been used to target political opposition, dissolve civil society groups and silence independent media.

articles.title: Ex-law dean withdraws as defense witness in Sara Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: A former law school dean who was invited by the team of Vice President Sara Duterte has declined to testify for the defense.

blocks.text: November 5, 2026 | 10:59am
The Senate impeachment court votes on the threshold required to convict an impeachable official on Sept. 23, 2026, with 13 senator-judges voting in favor and one against.
Senate of the Philippines / Joseph Vidal via Facebook
MANILA, Philippines — A former law school dean who was invited by the team of Vice President Sara Duterte has declined to testify for the defense.

In a statement on Thursday, November 5, former University of St. La Salle College of Law dean Ralph Sarmiento said that he was declining the defense panel’s invitation to “preserve the independence” of his “constitutional law scholarship” and the impartiality of his legal views and opinions.
“I had not anticipated that these views might potentially become part of the impeachment proceedings,” Sarmiento said.
“After careful consideration, I have decided to decline participation as a witness in the proceedings,” he added.
Sarmiento said that he had already reached out to the defense team, asking it to withdraw its request for a subpoena or his appearance.
The former law school dean was supposed to be the first witness to be presented by the defense team.

In their manifestation, Duterte’s defense team said that Sarmiento was expected to provide testimony regarding legal and constitutional principles relevant to the case, with a specific focus on Article II of the Articles of Impeachment.

Article II accuses Duterte of culpable violation of the Constitution and betrayal of public trust over her alleged unexplained wealth, discrepancies in her Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs), and alleged failure to divest from business interests while serving as vice president.
Duterte’s defense team cited Sarmiento’s credentials as a professor of Political and Constitutional Law as evidence of his capacity as a witness.
The defense team’s spokesperson, Michael Poa, said that the panel respects his decision.
“We respect Dean Sarmiento’s personal decision and appreciate his initial consideration of our invitation,” Poa said.
“We wish him well in his continued contributions to constitutional discourse,” he added.
Other witnesses are also expected to be disclosed in subsequent filings for hearings scheduled for November 10, 11, 12, 13, 19, 20 and 23.

articles.title: Pope Leo hosts Bob Dylan at official residence in Rome
articles.summary: Pope Leo had previously quoted Dylan's work in the preface of a book warning against nuclear rearmament.

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV hosted Bob Dylan at his official residence, the Apostolic Palace, on Wednesday during the Rome stop on the singer-songwriter's Italian tour.
Dylan, 85, wore a nearly all-black outfit, including a pulled up hoodie, gloves and umbrella, starkly contrasting with the Chicago-born Pope's all-white vestments.
The meeting between the pair, who both hail from the US Midwest, was brief, according to Vatican News.
Leo presented the Nobel laureate with a rosary and Dylan gifted Leo a copy of his autobiography, Chronicles: Volume One.
The visit happened ahead of Dylan's scheduled performance on Thursday at the Palazzo dello Sport, one of several Italian stops on his Rough and Rowdy Ways tour.
Leo has previously referenced Dylan in his own work, quoting Dylan's unreleased anti-nuclear song, Go Away You Bomb, in the preface to a book titled Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift.
"I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an' man-handled," was the line quoted in the book's warning to the world against rearmament.

The song was written in 1963 amid the Cold War, but was never recorded. The typewritten lyrics were unpublished until 2013 when they were discovered and put up for auction, according to the New York Times.
It was the second time Dylan had met a pope. In 1997 Dylan was invited to perform in front of Pope John Paul II and about 300,000 young people for the 23rd National Eucharistic Congress in Bologna.
Dylan played four songs including Knockin' on Heaven's Door, and reportedly climbed the stage mid-set to greet John Paul with a handshake and exchange a few words.
The then-Pope quoted Dylan's hit Blowin' in the Wind in his sermon to the crowd.

articles.title: Former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon enters witness box in Sydney double murder trial
articles.summary:
Lamarre-Condon gives evidence in court after pleading not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in early 2024

blocks.text: Former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon is giving evidence from the witness box in his double murder trial as his defence begins in Sydney.
Lamarre-Condon, 31, is accused of fatally shooting couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Lamarre-Condon on Thursday started giving evidence at the New South Wales supreme court in front of a 15-person jury. He was the first witness for the defence.
Wearing a light grey suit, a dark coloured tie and a white collared shirt, Lamarre-Condon vowed to tell the truth.

Prosecution lawyers wrapped up their case on Thursday morning. They called more than 50 witnesses, played hours of CCTV footage and shared pages of social media messages over the first seven weeks of the trial.
Lamarre-Condon’s defence team has previously claimed Baird and Davies were accidentally shot in two separate struggles with the accused when he was acting in “self-defence”.
The officer cleaned up the scene and disposed of the bodies afterwards because he “panicked considerably”, the defence lawyer John Stratton SC previously said.

articles.title: Former NASA chief economist named new head of Canadian Space Agency
articles.summary: Alexander MacDonald was named the new president of the Canadian Space Agency late Wednesday evening.

image.caption: The Canadian Space Agency’s David Florida Laboratory is seen in Ottawa on March 16. Alexander MacDonald was named the agency's new president on Wednesday. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Alexander MacDonald was named the new president of the Canadian Space Agency late Wednesday evening.
Alexander MacDonald helped establish the 'Moon to Mars' strategy that includes the Artemis mission
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly made the announcement in Ottawa during a tribute event to the late Marc Garneau, the first Canadian to travel to space.

MacDonald served as NASA's first chief economist, according to a government news release. In that role, he helped establish the "Moon to Mars" strategy, which includes the recent Artemis II mission that saw Canadian Jeremy Hansen travel around the moon earlier this year.
"As incredible as this year has been, I am even more excited about what the future holds for Canadians in space," MacDonald told the Ottawa crowd at Thursday's event.
"Space has never been more important for the strength and future of Canada, and never before has the world looked to Canada more for global leadership in the space domain."

items: Canada can't launch rockets on its own. A handful of companies want to change that

blocks.text: MacDonald takes over from Campbell

MacDonald is taking over from outgoing president Lisa Campbell, who had been in the role since 2020. His appointment comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney's government looks to expand Canada's space capabilities.
Earlier this month, Joly also appointed Hansen as a special advisor to the government on developing a new space strategy.

The federal government listed space-based platforms for surveillance as a key priority in its new defence industrial strategy released in February. The Carney government is also looking to expand co-operation with European countries in space as part of the proposed partnership with the European Union.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Judge rejects grandparent scammer's bid to back out of guilty plea, sends her to jail instead
articles.summary: A Calgary woman who admitted to stealing thousands of dollars from elderly victims was handed a 12-month jail sentence plus a year of probation after the judge refused to allow her to back out of her…

image.caption: Alana Duncan pleaded guilty to seven counts of fraud over $5,000 for her role in a grandparent scam. (Calgary Police Service)

blocks.text: Calgary

A Calgary woman who admitted to stealing thousands of dollars from elderly victims was handed a 12-month jail sentence plus a year of probation after the judge refused to allow her to back out of her guilty plea.
Alana Love Duncan, 48, pleaded guilty to seven counts of fraud over $5,000

Alana Love Duncan, 48, pleaded guilty last year to seven counts of fraud over $5,000 after she and several accomplices stole about $70,000 from seven women, who were mostly in their eighties and nineties, over a four-week period in the summer of 2023.

The “sophisticated and predatory” grandparent scam involved Duncan acting as an “in-person courier,” noted prosecutor Don Couturier at a sentencing hearing earlier this year. In each case, the victim received a call with news that her grandson, great-grandson or nephew was in trouble and needed money.
Duncan is the only one who has been charged.
Following her plea, the Crown and defence jointly proposed a conditional sentence for Duncan, meaning she would serve her sentence at home under conditions including house arrest and then curfew.
'She stood face to face with these people'
Defence lawyer Mary Stephensen had told the judge that Duncan had been addicted to crack cocaine but was sober and focused on “trying to right this wrong.”

items: Woman who stole $70K in grandparent scam should get house arrest, lawyers argue

blocks.text: But in her June decision to reject the conditional sentence, Court of King’s Bench Justice Michele Hollins noted that Duncan is currently unemployed and living at home, receiving government assistance.
The proposed sentence, said Hollins, “would look very similar to the life she is living pre-conviction” and wouldn't “be at all acceptable to a reasonably informed member of the public.”
“She stood face to face with these people and took their money, knowing they believed they had to give it to her to help a family member in trouble,” wrote Hollins.
"Approving this conditional sentence would not sufficiently denounce these crimes."
Attempt to back out of plea
When she learned she would be facing a jail term, Duncan then applied to vacate her guilty plea.
On Wednesday, Hollins rejected that application, finding the proper avenue is an appeal.
Hollins then handed Duncan a one-year sentence, followed by a year of probation and ordered her to pay $12,000 in restitution.
Coin collection handed over
“The vulnerability that was exploited here was familial,” wrote Hollins in her earlier decision.
The victims were instructed to keep the matter private.
They then went to their bank and withdrew between $6,500 and $10,000 in cash, handing it over to Duncan when she arrived to collect.
In one case, a 94-year-old victim did not have the $8,000 she believed was needed for her great-grandson’s bail, so she gave away her coin collection worth $22,000.
Duncan was the one who took the coins.
“These fraudsters impersonated the grandchildren and great grandchildren of these victims, even in one case saying 'I love you lots,'" wrote Hollins.
“They also impersonated the police or other law enforcement persons, again taking extreme advantage of the trust people generally put in law enforcement.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Meghan Grant is a justice affairs reporter. She has been covering courts, crime and stories of police accountability in southern Alberta for more than 15 years. Send Meghan a story tip at meghan.grant@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Filipino teens among least physically active globally — WHO study
articles.summary: Around 40% of Filipino adolescents reported no day with at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity in a week

blocks.text: November 5, 2026 | 9:26am
MANILA, Philippines — About two in five Filipino adolescents reported getting less than an hour of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, falling behind their counterparts around the world.
The World Health Organization's latest survey foudn tha taround 40% of adolescents aged 11 to 17 in the Philippines reported having no "active day" in a week.
An active day was defined as one with at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, such as brisk walking, cycling, playing sports or other activities that raise the heart rate.
The study, published in The Lancet Global Health, draws on hundreds of population-based surveys from 140 countries and territories, involving more than 3.2 million teens.

The Philippines was grouped with Namibia and Nepal, where around 40% of adolescents also reported no active days. By comparison, the global average was about 25%. This makes the Philippines' youth among the least active in the world.
Over the years, overall inactivity barely changed and even marginally declined in the Philippines, from 40.85% in 2010 to 40.32% in 2025.
Filipino girls are even less active than their male counterparts in the 2025 findings, with 42.7% reporting having no active day compared with 38% of boys.
The trend is similar globally. Only 11% of girls said they were active every day, compared with 17% of boys.
"For 15 years, the world has made almost no progress in getting young people moving, and girls are being left furthest behind," WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.
PHILIPPINES | WORLD HEALTH ORGANIZATION DATA
4 in 10 Filipino adolescents report zero active days
Percentage of adolescents reporting no physically active days in the previous week, 2021–2025
Source: World Health Organization, physical activity data, Philippines, 2021–2025.
Global progress stalls
Worldwide, one in four adolescents aged 11 to 17 reported no active days in the previous week, according to estimates published in The Lancet Global Health.
That amounts to around 240 million young people.
The study drew on 389 population-based surveys from 140 countries and territories involving more than 3.2 million adolescents.
On average, adolescents reported being active for 2.7 days a week, while only 14% said they were active for at least 60 minutes on all seven days.
The WHO warned that physical inactivity is a major risk factor for heart disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers.
"Helping young people develop active habits early in life is critical to protecting their health and reducing the global burden of these diseases," the agency said.
The study found little global progress over the past 15 years, with adolescent physical activity levels remaining virtually unchanged since 2010.
More than individual choice
The WHO said physical activity depends partly on the environments in which adolescents live, study and travel.

Access to safe public spaces, opportunities to walk or cycle, transportation systems, school environments, affordability and social norms can all affect how active young people are. Increasingly screen-centered lifestyles may also play a role.
"The answer is not to tell adolescents to try harder. It is to build schools, streets and communities where moving, playing and being active is safe, easy and normal," Tedros said.
The WHO called for stronger action across education, transport, urban planning, sports and health to make physical activity easier and safer for young people.
"Countries need policies that make physical activity an easy, safe and accessible part of everyday life," the agency said. — Camille Diola with Agence France Presse

articles.title: Beach weather in November? In Canada? These photos prove it
articles.summary: Parts of Ontario and Quebec have been experiencing record-setting temperatures this week, and people have been taking full advantage of it.

image.caption: A woman stands in the St. Lawrence River at Verdun Beach as temperatures soar in Montreal on Wednesday. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada·Photos
Parts of Ontario and Quebec have been experiencing record-setting temperatures this week, and people have been taking full advantage of it.
Parts of Ontario and Quebec have been basking in summer-like weather this week
Even at the best of times, it's hard to imagine swimming outdoors in November — no matter where you live in Canada. But 2026 is changing that conventional wisdom.
Parts of Quebec and Ontario have been experiencing potentially record-setting summer-like temperatures this week, with highs over 20 C.
Normal highs in major cities this time of year are around 10 C.
In Montreal on Wednesday, it was 22 C, but felt like 24 C. Good enough for a trip to the beach.
A woman enjoys the warm weather at Verdun Beach in Montreal on Wednesday. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

According to the Weather Network, the weather anomaly is due to a strong, high-pressure ridge off the U.S. East Coast and a warm front associated with a Colorado low — a low-pressure area caused by the Rocky Mountains that tends to track northeastward. Those systems combined are pushing warmer air into parts of Canada.
Toronto has also been warmer than normal.
With a high around 21 C in Toronto Wednesday, some people took to a hammock to enjoy the sunshine. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press)
Wearing shorts in Toronto in November? Why not? This man took advantage of the warmth as he walked his dogs Tuesday. (Alex Lupul/CBC)
What’s behind the warm November weather in London?
El Niño effect
This year's strong El Niño is probably part of the story, too.
Bill Merryfield, a research scientist at Environment and Climate Change Canada, says El Niño usually affects Canada toward the end of the year, causing unusually mild fall and winter temperatures.

"This year's event is truly exceptional because this warming has already exceeded three degrees, which is well above that of any previous event and is expected to go even higher before the usual peak of El Niño in November or December," he said, referring to Pacific Ocean temperatures tied to the weather phenomenon.
Two people take a break on Parliament Hill during an unseasonably warm Nov. 4. (Dan Taekema/CBC)
It was a warm day under the fall foliage at Toronto's High Park. (Alex Lupul/CBC)
A cyclist in Toronto took advantage of the delayed start of cooler temps, too. (Alex Lupul/CBC)
People had the same idea in western Quebec, too.
With files from The Canadian Press

articles.title: Hubert Aiwanger, prominent German politician, found dead in Berlin hotel
articles.summary:
Police and prosecutors open investigation into death of the 55-year-old Bavarian state deputy leader

A prominent German politician was found dead in a Berlin hotel on Wednesday, police said,…

blocks.text: A prominent German politician was found dead in a Berlin hotel on Wednesday, police said, adding they had launched an investigation.
The cause of death of Hubert Aiwanger, 55, who was deputy leader of southern Bavaria state, was not immediately clear.
Police said in a statement he was “found dead in his hotel room” in the Berlin-Mitte district.
Police and prosecutors had opened a probe to “determine the specific cause and circumstances of death”, the statement said.

“The aim ⁠of the inquest is to establish the ​specific cause of death ‌and the ‌circumstances surrounding it, and to rule out any ‌possible third-party culpability,” police and prosecutors said in a statement. They gave no further details.

Aiwanger, head of the populist Free Voters party and also Bavarian economy minister, was in Berlin to attend the opening of an office for his party but missed the event as he was feeling unwell, the Bild daily reported.
His body was later discovered by police in the hotel, it said.
The Bavarian state premier, Markus Soeder, described Aiwanger’s death as an “absolute tragedy”.
“We are all deeply shocked. Our thoughts are now first and foremost with his family and his children,” he said.
Aiwanger’s party were junior partners in the regional Bavarian government led by Soeder’s Christian Social Union (CSU).

He had headed the Bavarian branch of the Free Voters since 2006. Under his leadership, the party made it into the state government for the first time in 2018, but never won enough seats to qualify for Germany’s federal parliament.
Aiwanger had faced national controversy in 2023 after reports emerged that he wrote an antisemitic pamphlet as a 17-year-old schoolboy, in which Auschwitz was described as an “entertainment quarter”.
He denied having written the pamphlet, though he has admitted to having had “one or a few copies” of it in his school bag. He apologised over the affair but refused to step down.
Aiwanger had two children and lived with his partner, German media reported.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters
